questions.q: What is the process that caused the formation of the Himalayan mountain range?
questions.a: The Himalayas formed when the Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks mountains just "appeared" or were made by volcanic activity, missing the concept of plate movement.

questions.q: Why do we describe the Himalayas as the "youngest" mountain range in the world?
questions.a: They are called "youngest" because they formed relatively recently (about 50 million years ago) compared to ancient mountain ranges, and they are still rising. If a student thinks "youngest" means they were formed yesterday, they miss the geological timescale of millions of years.

questions.q: If you were travelling from the northernmost point of India towards the plains, which of the three parallel ranges would you encounter first?
questions.a: You would encounter the Greater Himalayas (Himadri) first. A wrong answer reveals a failure to understand the North-to-South arrangement of the ranges.

questions.q: How does the height of the Greater Himalayas affect the weather in India?
questions.a: The height acts as a barrier that prevents cold winds from Central Asia from entering India. A wrong answer shows the student hasn't linked physical features (mountains) to their impact on climate.

questions.q: Is the height of the Himalayas fixed forever? Support your answer.
questions.a: No, they are not fixed because the tectonic plates are still colliding, causing the mountains to rise by a few millimetres each year. A wrong answer suggests the student views the earth as static and unchanging.

questions.q: Imagine if the Himalayas were a flat plateau instead of high mountains. How would life in Northern India change?
questions.a: The answer should explain that India would lose its protection from cold northern winds and the water source for major rivers. A poor answer focuses only on scenery rather than the vital climate/water impact.
